items.title: Could 71km of time trialing actually help Remco Evenepoel win the Tour de France? A closer look at exactly what the Belgian could gain against Pogačar
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Not since Bradley Wiggins won the 2012 Tour de France have there been as many individual time trial kilometres on the route of cycling's biggest race, with the 71km included on the 2027 route swinging the balance towards the best ITT rider in the peloton and four-time World Champion Remco Evenepoel.

While no route can really be anti-Tadej Pogačar, this is about as good as it can get for the Belgian, with only three summit finishes and almost all of the hardest climbs being backloaded in the second two thirds of the route. Runner-up in 2026 to the Slovenian, Evenepoel will surely be back at the Tour in July, with his eye on at least a repeat GC performance.

Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe team boss Ralph Denk didn't go over the top with his assessment of the route and the advantages Evenepoel might seek to gain, but it is clear that a more TT-heavy Grand Tour will always suit his attributes.

"A dream Tour profile for Remco Evenepoel? Hmm, I see that a little differently. More nuanced," he said to at the presentation in Paris, before conceding that, on paper at least, stages 7 and 16 being mostly flat races against the clock should play into their hands.

"In 2012, when Bradley Wiggins won, there were even more than 100. But anyway, it's not bad at all for us, let's say. Remco is currently the very best time trialist in the world, so that is an aspect of this Tour we are certainly going to take into account. That he can gain time on Pogačar, Vingegaard, Seixas and co. in those? In theory, yes."

"The multiple time trial kilometres will provide an extra dimension in any case and make the battle for the yellow jersey more open and exciting," said team Chief of Sports Zak Dempster in agreement.

But how much could the return to more than 70km of individual time trialling – for the first time in 14 years – really benefit Evenepoel in the fight against Pogačar?

Evenepoel only made his Tour debut in 2024, so the three editions he has taken on against the now five-time champion and joint record holder Pogačar have only brought them up against each other in five Grand Tour time trials.

All of those being at the Tour, the score for the moment is 3-2 in the favour of the Belgian, with Pogačar winning the two most climbing-packed stages against the clock in Nice at the end of the 2024 race, and on the pure mountain ITT to Peyragudes in 2025.

Evenepoel has beaten Pogačar to three stage wins at the flatter tests in Gevrey-Chambertin in 2024, Caen in 2025, and Thonon-les-Bains this past season, but the margin has never been major – 12 seconds, 16 seconds, and 28 seconds.

Yes, he has had the advantage – as he should on the completely flat stage 7 to Chambord and stage 16 in Toulouse, even with the viciously steep Côte de Pech David (800m at 12.%) characterising the middle of the route – but it's far from the complete domination that Evenepoel has subjected everyone, including Pogačar, to outside of the Grand Tours.

The image of Evenepoel riding past the usually immortal Slovenian's green jersey during the time trial at the World Championships in Kigali 13 months ago is one which will serve as a symbol of the Belgian's absolute monopoly over the discipline in recent memory, claiming the past four rainbow jerseys.

On that day, the monumental gap between their TT abilities wasn't only apparent in the overtake, but in the time difference at the finish: 2:37.

In fact, across their careers, they have faced off 12 times in individual time trials, Evenepoel winning 10 of them. Only on the two mountain courses at the Tour has he lost to Pogačar to against the clock.

So why does the gap seem to narrow significantly when they are racing in a time trial in the Tour?

The balance swinging massively in Pogačar's favour when an uphill road is included is no surprise – with less aerodynamic advantage for the 'Aero Bullet' Evenepoel at play, due to drag becoming less of a factor at slower speeds, and power-to-weight ratio (W/kg) becoming the more important variable.

But even on the flatter and purer courses, where Evenepoel has long been putting the likes of two-time World Champion Filippo Ganna to shame – most recently by a relatively huge 57 seconds at Worlds in Montreal, Pogačar is much closer during the Tour.

The likely answer comes down to weight, with Evenepoel admitting just this year that he arrived at the Tour almost 4kg down on the weight he had been operating at during the Classics. It's no secret that Evenepoel was in incredible condition for this year's Tour, putting up some of his best climbing performances with victory atop Plateau de Solaison, second on Alpe d'Huez, and keeping up with Pogačar for much longer in the second and third weeks than he has in previous years.

For events like the Worlds TT, where he destroyed Pogačar in Kigali as mentioned, Evenepoel operates at a higher weight, gaining around 1-2kg and losing some of his power-to-weight ratio as he ups the raw power numbers for his favoured discipline.

There's also the factor that no one in the peloton can maintain their level over three weeks like six-time Grand Tour winner Pogačar, whose repeatability and powers of recovery make him the perfect rider to take on punchy finishes, mountain stages and time trials day after day at the Tour – and compete for the win on all of them.

The best benchmark we have for how much time Evenepoel gain across 71 kilometres of time trials is the 28-second deficit he opened up to Pogačar at this year's Tour, over a course of just 26.1km.

Based on their average speeds from that day, 48.85kph for Evenepoel and 47.751kph for Pogačar, a perfect world would see the Belgian cover the 71km 1:05 faster than his rival – not exactly world-beating, but a time trial, with corners, ups and downs, and several accelerations, is far from a perfect world.

Evenepoel's advantage could become greater the longer they have to race, given he has the best aero TT position in the peloton, especially with the 71km being split into a flatter 38km effort, where the Belgian's edge should be magnified as the kilometres tick by. But the steep hill on stage 16 also plays massively into the hands of Pogačar, even at just 800 metres in length, equalising the equation between the pair. ]

The clear conclusion is that Evenepoel cannot rely just on his strongest weapon to truly take down the current benchmark – he will have to beat him, or, at the bare minimum, match him in the high mountains to stay in striking distance for the stages he will almost definitely win.

One other factor that the Belgian newspaper put to Red Bull management is how the arrival of the first mountain stage on stage 9 could help Evenepoel, who really built into his climbing powers this past July after struggling in the opening week.

"That can indeed be an advantage," said Denk. "On the other hand: if you go all out for the general classification, and that is what we always want to do with this team, you also have to be alert in those first ten days and control the situation."

Of his eventual 6:26 deficit to Pogačar in Paris, Evenepoel lost almost three minutes of that on stage 6, the first real big mountain day to Gavarnie-Gèdre. Losing just over three minutes over the remaining 15 stages was a massive step up, and could also play into the hands of the ever-developing Belgian star in his second year with Red Bull, but he'll have to cling onto Pogačar's wheel on stages like the brutal 18th to Col du Portet in a way that only really Jonas Vingegaard has been able to do since 2020 if he wants any hope of yellow.

items.title: 'The race will be wide open' – With no long climbs and no individual time trial, does the 2027 Tour de France Femmes route suit home favourite Pauline Ferrand-Prévot?
items.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
items.content:
Two summers ago, Pauline Ferrand-Prévot soared to a historic home victory at the Tour de France Femmes, dominating the closing Alpine stages to deliver a first French Tour win in decades and the biggest win of her career.

She beat Demi Vollering by almost four minutes in Châtel, but this year the tables turned as Ferrand-Prévot endured a disastrous title defence, losing minutes in the Dijon time trial before falling out of contention in the Ardèche hills and conceding defeat on Mont Ventoux.

Clearly, a rider of Ferrand-Prévot's calibre is better than her early-August performance, and the Visma-Lease a Bike star will aim to bounce back next year. But is the 2027 Tour de France Femmes route one where she can thrive and take back the yellow jersey from Vollering?

Well, race director Marion Rousse delivered both good and bad news for the 34-year-old and her team in the Palais des Congrès in Paris on Thursday afternoon.

For a start, there's no individual time trial on next year's route. That will be music to Ferrand-Prévot's ears after she lost two minutes to Vollering and Marlen Reusser over just 21km on the road to Dijon in August.

Ferrand-Prévot was always expected to shed time against the clock, even as her team protested how much she had trained on the TT bike, so for a start, she's already looking at several minutes saved. Coming in place of an individual time trial, however, is a team test in the form of a flat 18km tour of central London.

Team time trials are rare in women's cycling, with next year's stage a first in Tour de France Femmes history. The other Grand Tours have featured a TTT in recent history, though, with the Giro featuring one in 2021 and the Vuelta doing so between 2022 and 2025.

Do Visma have the personnel to succeed in such a test? Time will tell, and it's impossible to make any predictions this far out, but in former time trial specialist Jos van Emden, they have a directeur sportif well-placed to guide them in London.

"The team time trial is a notable feature. It’s an event we haven't seen before in the Tour de France Femmes," Van Emden said after the route unveiling.

"I'm a fan of team time trials. We haven't raced many of them as a team, so it's difficult to make any immediate predictions about our collective strength or the course in London. You have to master every discipline if you want to win the Tour. This will be another new challenge.

"That decision shows that women's cycling is continuing to evolve and grow in importance. A team time trial is part of what makes the Tour the Tour, as it’s the biggest stage in cycling."

Is there enough climbing for PFP?

The goal will likely be to limit losses and keep Ferrand-Prévot close to her main yellow jersey rivals as the race hits France, with the opening two stages in the north of England unlikely to have produced much in the way of GC gaps.

On the mainland, it will all be about surviving the pitfalls of the sprint stages and then overcoming the tricky, punchy hills on the road to Magnanville on stage 5.

The big time differences, however, should be made in the final three days as the race reaches the Massif Central, though there are no long Alpine climbs on the menu here like the Madeleine, where Ferrand-Prévot built her 2025 Tour victory with that dominant solo ride.

Will that be a problem for the lightweight climber?

"The first thing that stands out to me is how different this Tour is from the editions in recent years. The high mountains are missing. That was certainly different in previous editions," Van Emden said.

Stage 7 features a closing climb to La Loge des Gardes (6.7km at 7.1%), while the mid-mountain stage 8 to Clermont-Ferrand features the Côte de Charade (6km at 5.9%) before a descent to the finish. The showpiece final stage concludes atop the Puy de Dôme, which measures 11.3km at an average gradient of 7.8%.

Van Emden said that the Tour is no easier than the recent editions, even if the Puy de Dôme stage doesn't quite measure up to the recent queen stages of the Glandon-Alpe d'Huez in 2024, the Madeleine last year, or the Ventoux in August.

"The longest climb in this Tour is 11km. That was different in recent years. But that doesn’t mean this will be an easier Tour," he said.

"Quite the opposite: the race will be wide open, and the general classification contenders will be fighting for every second in every stage.

"That’s a very special way to finish. In cycling, this climb may not be as well known as Mont Ventoux or the Col de la Madeleine, which featured in recent editions, but that’s also because it’s a protected natural area. I’m really looking forward to finishing atop the volcano."

As is the case for the men's race, there's clearly one standout favourite for next year's Tour de France Femmes – the defending champion. This Tour route certainly isn't built with Ferrand-Prévot in mind, but success isn't out of reach, and if she's back on form, next August could well host the Ferrand-Prévot vs Vollering battle we've been waiting for.

Between now and then, there's plenty of time for training, planning, and recon rides. The planning will get underway soon, said Van Emden.

"We’ll draw up our plans this winter. With Pauline, we have the 2025 Tour winner on our team, although she would normally be better suited to the longer climbs.

"But we have several cards to play. I think this route suits us very well. It’s going to be an explosive Tour."

items.title: 'It's a question of resetting the balance' – Tour de France boss namechecks Bradley Wiggins and Federico Bahamontes to explain major increase in time trialling on 2027 route
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
Tour de France director Christian Prudhomme delved deep into the race's own history books to explain exactly why organisers have opted in 2027 to make the biggest increase in time trialling in the route in 15 years

Instead, Prudhomme cited time trialling star Bradley Wiggins, who conquered Britain's first Tour de France in 2012, and the rider voted the race's greatest ever climber, 1959 winner Federico Martín Bahamontes, to explain the TT increase.

Rather than looking back at just the last three editions of the race, where Tadej Pogačar has effectively made the battle for the yellow jersey a one-man show, Prudhomme used a much bigger context to explain what provides the chance – though it's far from guaranteed – for a radical switch in the balance of power between TT specialists and climbers

"The reason is simple, although we should put things into perspective, given we're in a world where people don't put things into perspective anymore," Prudhomme told reporters at the presentation, which revealed there'll be a 38-kilometre time trial on stage 7 and a 33-kilometre TT on stage 11.

"It's been 15 years since we've had so much time trialling, during the Tour won by Bradley Wiggins, and this is done with that in mind.

"Since then the riders who won in the time trials have also won in the mountains so it made no sense to extend the TT distances because the same people won, anyway.

"But now that's not the case, we've got different kinds of riders. It's just like back in the very distant era when Federico Bahamontes took time [in the mountains] on Jacques Anquetil," a renowned time trialling specialist.

"Now it's Remco Evenepoel who gains time against the clock, which he may lose in the mountains."

"It's not anti-Tadej Pogačar"

Prudhomme's comments about Bahamontes and Anquetil regarding balance could also have referred to the 1959 Tour, won by the Eagle of Toledo in part thanks to his crushing domination in a mountain time trial on the Puy de Dôme, where riders like Anquetil were pushed to nearly four minutes back. That said, Anquetil then regained more than five on Bahamontes in the race's final TT to Dijon, a massive 69 kilometres long. But there was some kind of balance, even if Bahamontes had done more than enough to win the Tour outright by that point.

In either case, Prudhomme argued, if Evenepoel was an example for now, it wasn't simply designed to favour one rider in particular. Rather, the question of having a much higher number of time trialling kilometres in 2027 was mainly to ensure that rather than any rider gaining too much of an advantage early on, the suspense could be maintained as long as possible.

"It's a question of resetting the balance, not for the organisers but all the fans who want there to be a fight right the way to the end," Prudhomme explained.

"It's not anti-Tadej Pogačar, you put pavé or time trials or climbs in front of him, he can take time and then he gains even more time on his rivals on the descents," he added, in reference to what Pogačar did on the descent of the Tourmalet on stage 6 last July, doubling his advantage over Jonas Vingegaard after dropping him close to the summit and all but winning the Tour in the process.

"If he [Pogačar] is stronger, he's stronger," Prudhomme added. "But there is a will to rebalance things, not for a single rider in particular, just like a few years ago we tried to make the route have a more punchy kind of course to try to boost the chances of a spectacular race.

"But in any case," Prudhomme concluded, making a wordplay on an old proverb, "the organisers propose and the riders dispose. That's always true."

"There are a lot of really tough unknown or semi-unknown climbs in this Tour"

While the increase in time trialling kilometres represented one big change in route trends, Prudhomme argued that the fans should not take it for granted that the mountains in the 2027 race would be a straightforward re-run of other years.

"I hope that people will be surprised, first on paper, then after being surprised on paper, in reality. Because there are a lot of really tough unknown or semi-unknown climbs in this Tour, and others which have been around but which don't have as fearsome a reputation as they deserve," he told reporters.

"So it's true we've got some classic climbs like the Tourmalet. But I'm thinking especially of the return of the Col de Burdincurutcheta, which is one of the hardest in the French Basque Country," he said of the early climb on stage 19, 8.7km long with average gradients of 9.3%.

"Then the Col du Pré, which is really daunting, too," he added of the Alpine climb, measuring 12.6km at 7.8%, which appears before the final ascent of Saisies on stage 11.

"Then there is the stage across the Massif Central with more than 3,800 metres of vertical climbing through beautiful but tough landscapes.

"Don't forget, too, that in the first week we're in Wales, there are climbs that are really hard, right from the gun on stage 3. I know the local people there are very proud of what will be on show in their part of the world that day."

One unusual feature of the Tour de France is its mini-homage to the 2027 UCI Cycling World Championships, the so-called 'Super Worlds', which will take place on the road in the northern Alps in late August and on the track in the Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines velodrome near Paris.

Stage 10 will feature the circuit of the Côte de Domancy and finishes in Sallanches, where the road World Championships also took place in 1980 and will do again in 2027, whilst stage 21 starts in Saint-Quentin-en-Yvelines and will go past the velodrome en route to the Champs-Élysées.

"We weren't going ever to do the World Championships before the World Championships actually took place, which is why there will only be two ascents of the Domancy and not 20," Prudhomme explained, "but that's where Bernard Hinault, a legend of the Tour, won the Worlds in 1980, so it's also to honour him."

"The climbs there aren't very high up, but the slopes are something special: short but really, really tough. So there will be lots to see that day, too."

And perhaps, too, in the time trials as well.

items.title: "It's pretty bad" – Why Norris needs headache tablets for bumpy Austin circuit
The Knicks finally got their rings, the coaches got boxes
items.author: Russell Richardson
items.content:
Imagine your employer had an excellent year and you were in line for an award, one you earned through great effort, extensive travel, and long nights. Instead of receiving it, however, you’re handed an IOU note at the ceremony. Or worse, you were with a fake email about the award, just to test the company’s cybersecurity.

When Vardon describes this very scenario in his latest report, he’s not talking about the slighted workers of a local plumbing supply company. He’s talking about the assistant coaches and staff of the world champion New York Knicks.

At Tuesday’s season opener, the presentation (broadcast nationally on NBC) made it appear the Knicks assistant coaches were receiving championship rings during the pregame banner ceremony. The boxes they were handed? Empty.

It came as no surprise to the assistants. They hadn’t even been fitted for rings, and the empty boxes were a token gesture so they wouldn’t feel left out. Token gestures can backfire on you, though, especially when they seem, perhaps, insincere. The Knicks coaches were upset, according to Vardon, on a scale from mild irritation to very spicy.

In quintessential Knicks fashion, the organization’s statement on the situation is, “We are not disclosing anything about the rings.” Because robots need not acknowledge the petty concerns of disposable humans.

One of the most stunning quotes from Vardon’s piece is this:

“ received conflicting information about whether head coach Mike Brown received his ring on Tuesday and could not immediately verify if he got one.”

What? We can’t confirm if coach Mike Brown got a ring?

The story careens off a cliff from there. Vardon notes, “Many longtime employees at Madison Square Garden, including some who work in the Knicks’ business operations, will not receive rings at all […]. Typically, most employees for NBA teams receive rings, even if they are not as fancy and expensive as the ones the players receive.” Yes, some franchises reward the plebes, but not the NBA’s second-most valuable one. Enter Gordon Gekko, stage left.

However, in September, MSG sent employees a fake championship ring offer. The email congratulated recipients and invited them to select one of two complimentary ring designs: “Championship Gold” or “Garden Classic.” But The email was actually an internal phishing test. Employees who clicked the link were assigned mandatory cybersecurity training rather than receive a ring.

What kind of cold, villainous monster says, “You know how we’re not giving the employees championship rings? One hilarious way to test our cybersecurity would be….”

Oh, the team ain’t hurting for money. The Knicks reportedly generated $640 million in revenue during their championship season, while the franchise’s estimated valuation climbed 29% to $12.6 billion, making it the NBA’s second-most valuable team.

Giving New York the benefit of the doubt, those rings must be difficult to manufacture. Designed by Jason Arasheben of Jason of Beverly Hills, the Knicks’ blingy ring features roughly 800 diamonds and sapphires totaling 22 carats, set in white gold. Its elaborate design includes a mechanical pop-up replica of Madison Square Garden, 16 emerald-cut diamonds representing the team’s playoff victories, and a 0.16-carat diamond set in the Larry O’Brien Trophy. One cannot gaze for long upon the ring before weeping, and it must be returned to Mount Doom post haste!

The Knicks won in mid-June, leaving about four months for design, contract, and construction. That’s a tight schedule. Delays aren’t unprecedented in the NBA, and according to team sources, the assistants will eventually receive rings. Still, other championship teams have distributed coaches’ rings on opening night, so…

Who are we talking about, exactly? The championship coaching staff included associate head coach Chris Jent, assistants Rick Brunson, Mark Bryant, Darren Erman, Riccardo Fois, Brendan O’Connor, and TJ Saint, along with several player development coaches and advisors (including one of the greatest names in NBA history, the legendary Mo Cheeks!). These were among the people who helped deliver New York’s first NBA championship in 53 years.

To recap: What should have been a celebration of the Knicks’ victory instead exposed tiresome and familiar organizational dysfunction, with coaches handed empty boxes and longtime employees subjected to a misleading phishing exercise. Team owner James Dolan proves once again to be tone-deaf, and this time not by singing at the mic.

A franchise worth billions, a championship decades in the making, and apparently not enough goodwill to go around. How come they win it all and still feel like LOLKnicks?

Read Vardon’s full article here. Go Knicks.

items.title: Anti-Pogačar? Not quite, but this radical Tour de France route does highlight ASO's love-hate relationship with the world's best rider
items.author: Patrick Fletcher
items.content:
You might have seen the 2027 Tour de France route described as an 'anti-Pogačar' exercise, and, with a return to time trialling doses of old and a relatively meagre helping of high mountains, you can certainly see why.

In truth, there is no such thing as an 'anti-Pogačar' route. It simply does not exist within the realms of plausible conception. It would have to be 21 flat stages, half of them against the clock, and even then he’d still probably find a way to win.

And yet, the route that was unveiled in Paris on Thursday did signal a growing discomfort, on the part of the Tour de France organisers, with Tadej Pogačar’s dominance. Jonas Vingegaard’s epic takedowns of the Slovenian are three years in the past now, and Pogačar has since rattled off a trio of yellow jerseys, each more convincing than the last, to take his tally to a record-equalling five.

He has done so with the sort of panache the race directors can only dream of, but he has also done it with a level of ease that is becoming a bit of a nightmare. So utterly superior, Pogačar spent the second half of this year’s Tour essentially riding as a domestique for his third-placed teammate, Isaac del Toro. In some ways, the yellow jersey selflessly repaying favours is a nice image for the race. In others ways, it’s really not such a great look – not one you’d want to make a habit of, anyway.

The irony was that the 2026 Tour de France had been billed as a 'Tour of Suspense'. The route had been constructed in such a way, we were told, that the battle for yellow would only be decided in the final days on Alpe d’Huez. As it turned out, Pogačar had the jersey all but sewn up by stage 6.

I wrote a piece on this at the time – about how the attempt to tone down the early Col du Tourmalet only toned it up – so I won’t rehash it all here, but it was a bit of an own goal, I felt. Granted, Pogačar’s dominance would have told anyway, but in any case, it was revealing in the broader context of ASO’s intentions.

Put simply, they badly want a yellow jersey contest that remains open until the last few days, and it didn’t work last time.

Not a good year to be a polka-dot fan

And so here we are, not going above 1,750 metres of altitude until stage 18 of 21 next July.

The route for that stage is a Pyrenean beast – going over the Soulor, Tourmlaet, and Hourquette d’Ancizan before the final climb to the Col du Portet – but it makes everything else look pretty tame in comparison. In fact, it’s only the second of two true mountain-top finishes in the entire race.

The Alps have had it pretty good in recent years but what did they do to deserve this? Even if the World Champs-inspired stage 10 looks like a thriller and the stage 11 combo of the Col du Pré and Montée de Bisanne looks tough enough, the lack of big-name high-altitude Alpine passes is really quite shocking.

And the Pyrenees may have the upper hand this time but they too only have two stages. Elsewhere, it’s over to the Jura to provide the first summit finish on the Grand Colombier on stage 9, and the Massif Central on a stage 14 that is harder than it looks but still very much sloggy medium mountain stuff. All in all, then, not a good year to be a die-hard polka-dot fan.

And then there’s the time trialling, with 71km against the clock constituting the most ITT-heavy Tour de France since the former world TT champion Bradley Wiggins won the race in 2012. This itself is remarkable, a complete laying down of arms in the battle ASO has waged on time trialling over the past decade. This was, of course, inspired by the dominance of Team Sky – first through Wiggins and then through Chris Froome and Geraint Thomas – but the trend has remained even in the Pogačar and Vingegaard era.

Until now. It’s no coincidence that the runner-up this year is also the best time triallist in the world, by a country mile. Remco Evenepoel may well wear the yellow jersey in next year’s Tour, and he may well take a minute or two on Pogačar, though it’s worth remembering he was beaten by more than six this summer (with Pogačar taking his foot off the gas at times).

So you can’t Pogačar-proof a Tour de France route, but in completely upending the balance between mountains and time trials, the organisers have certainly taken a new, much bolder, step in attempting to prevent him completely running away with it.

Pro-Pogačar, anti-Vingegaard?

At this point, it’s worth circling back to ASO’s relationship with Pogačar, which we might describe as 'love-hate'. They hate the suspense he takes away from the race as a whole, but they absolutely love just about everything else about him.

Race director Christian Prudhomme and co barely made any attempt to hide their distaste of the so-called Skybots, and what an antidote they’ve since struck upon with Pogačar, an all-action figure who will light up the race given even the slightest invitation, or even the slightest hint of boredom. For two years in a row now he has been in the thick of the action on the remodelled final stage over the Montmartre climb in Paris, carrying the Classics torch that has seen him win Milan-San Remo, the Tour of Flanders, and twice podium Paris-Roubaix.

In that respect, this is actually quite a pro-Pogačar route. The entire first week is peppered with punchy climbs and Classics-flavoured stages that aren’t critical GC flashpoints but may well tempt Pogačar out to play. The first of the two Alpine stages, based on the route for World Championships past and future, looks like the sort of circuit-based, short-but-hard-climb affair Pogačar would draw up in his dreams.

The marquee high-mountain stages have been toned down only because the terrain dictates that this is where his superiority stretches into big time differences. But for all Pogačar is the best climber in the world, he’s not a pure climber, and he has famously come unstuck on some of the Tour’s most brutal mountain stages. Vingegaard was the man to crack him in both 2022 and 2023, and while the Dane hasn’t come close in recent years, he has mitigating circumstances, not least the fact that he didn’t get to finish this year’s race.

For many years now, Vingegaard has banged out the same old refrain – that he can only try and live with Pogačar on the punchier climbing days, and that he needs the bigger, heavier, multi-col mountain days to truly take the fight to him.

In that light, the 2027 Tour de France route only reduces the room for manouevre for the greatest rival of Pogačar’s career. Of course, with Paul Seixas coming through, that title could change hands at some point, and it’s worth noting that the French prodigy – already a winner at Il Lombardia and runner-up at Liège and Strade Bianche – is cut from very much the same cloth as Pogačar.

But no, if this route is anti-anyone, it’s anti-Vingegaard. And if you were the Dane, seeing your favored terrain neglected as Evenepoel’s is pandered to – by people who want a closer challenge to Pogačar – you might just take that personally.

As for main man himself, we return to the point we made at the start of this piece; you could devise 100 different Tour de France routes, and the Tadej Pogačar of the past three years would win every single time, provided he stays upright.

And here again Prudhomme made a revealing comment. "There are certainly questions lingering after his crash," the race director said of Pogačar’s season-ending Vuelta fall, even going as far as to reference Eddy Merckx’s famous (and much more severe) 1969 crash, after which he was supposedly never the same rider (but still won four more Tours). Prudhomme seems excited by that prospect of a slightly-less-than-perfect Pogačar, or at least relishing the doubt, the intrigue, the… suspense.

Whether we actually get any of the stuff next July remains to be seen. The Tour de France organisers love Tadej Pogačar, but they hate him too, and it seems even clearer now that they want the best of best worlds – to encourage his firework-lighting instincts while at the same time trying to rein him in to some degree.

In that respect, the 2027 Tour de France route is one of the most radical we’ve seen in years – it simply might not make a blind bit of difference.

items.title: 'I'm certainly not opposed to it' – Tim Merlier gives cautious thumbs up to teammate Paul Magnier joining him at 2027 Tour de France
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
Triple 2026 Tour de France stage winner Tim Merlier (Soudal-QuickStep) has given a cautious welcome to the idea that up-and-coming French sprinter and teammate Paul Magnier might join him in the 2027 race.

Next July, it might be that the two race together in a Grand Tour for the first time.

At the Tour presentation this Thursday, Merlier himself played down the number of sprint stages on offer in the 2027 route but he did not roundly reject the idea of sharing those opportunities with Merlier.

"I have already discussed that with the team," Merlier said in comments reported by . "I am certainly not opposed to it. I think it would be possible.

"He is still young and I have the feeling that he still looks up to me; he sometimes still asks for tips. He could learn a lot from it."

Although the Belgian star argued that it was not necessarily a given that it would happen, concluding on that subject – and without explaining why – that “the chance that it actually happens seems quite small to me".

The other big subject on the virtual table for Merlier in Paris was whether he could take the yellow jersey in Carlisle at the end of day 1 of the 2027 Tour. Opportunities for sprinters to take the opening stage's yellow jersey are never high in the Tour and the sprint finish in Carlisle is a gradual uphill, exactly the kind that Merlier likes.

Furthermore, after missing out in Lille in 2025, the previous chance the fast men had to go for yellow in the Tour, Merlier recognised that he was looking forward to a fresh chance coming his way.

“It would be wonderful. I let it slip in Lille in 2025, so I’m happy to get a second chance already. Normally, that doesn’t happen very often," he said.

"It's a nice challenge for the sprinters, and it's not impossible it could happen."

It might sound surprising that Merlier was pleased that there were two time trials in the 2027 route, but that was more for practical reasons because he was suddenly going to switch specialities at 33. At the same time, he agreed with Mark Cavendish that if the sprinters' teams worked well enough, the last day over the Butte Montmartre in Paris could still end up being decided by a mass dash to the line on the Champs Élysées.

"Two time trials are two rest days for me," he reasoned, "and though I'd like to see a 'real' sprint without the Montmartre on the last day, if the sprinters' teams all work well together, it might still be possible that it happens."

It is true, too, that stage 21 breakaway winner Mathieu van der Poel (Alpecin-Premier Tech) only took the last dash for the line in Paris by the bare minimum ahead of teammate Jasper Philipsen last July. But in any case, rather than the seven sprints predicted by the Tour de France organisation on Thursday for 2027, Merlier says that he thinks a much smaller number is likely.

"If we can sprint four times, that would already be great. It all looks very tough. When you see the elevation gain [53,450 metres - Ed.] across the race, you don't get very excited as a sprinter," he said with a laugh.

Game Preview: Knicks at Celtics, October 23, 2026
items.author: Moritz Wollert
items.content:
Remember the good old days of just caring about diamond rings, roughly 70 square feet of fabric and the feelings of Ariel Hukporti? Yeah, me neither. It’s what a loss against the Philadelphia 76ers on Banner Night at Madison Square Garden can do to you. It functions as a stark reminder that the new NBA season is upon us and the Knicks somehow have to find a way to let the past be the past and kick some serious you-know-what in the present. On Friday night in Boston, though, it will once again be hard to keep the nostalgia at bay. Even if Mitchell Robinson is not wearing the orange and blue anymore.

The former longest-tenured Knick has moved on to (not so) greener pastures and now starts for one of New York’s biggest rivals a good 200 miles up north. There’s probably no Knicks fan out there who won’t have some weird feeling in their stomach seeing the “Blockness Monster” in a uniform we’ve all been brought up to hate. And if I had to guess, I’d bet that Mr. Robinson puts in quite an effort on the glass tonight. Maybe Mitch even offers a glimpse of an expanded “bag,” as people like to call it these days. He’ll want to show his former team what they’re missing without him and prove to the Land of the Leprechauns that the $48 million they left for him at the end of the free agency rainbow wasn’t fool’s gold.

Celtics still love their three pointers

In Boston’s season opener, Mitch did not make a great impression on the C’s fanbase. Outside of Paul George, though, few players in green and white did. The Celtics lost at Detroit despite leading by 22 four minutes into the third quarter and by 10 with eight minutes left in the fourth. Somehow, someway, that sounds familiar, doesn’t it? And the Boston Celtics haven’t really changed that much from that incredibly entertaining playoff series they played with your beloved Bockers 17 months ago. Their personnel certainly changed, but in terms of their style of play, it’s still bombs away in Beantown.

Boston’s barrage of threes can overwhelm an opponent, just as it did against the Pistons for roughly three quarters on Tuesday, when the Celtics attempted 42 shots from downtown. Their shooting creates a lot of space to operate, puts a lot of stress on the opposing defense and can turn any game in an instant. That cuts both ways, though, because the Celtics really don’t care if they are up by 20 or down by 20. They just keep shooting, and sometimes they shoot themselves in the foot. They certainly did at Detroit, where they let a shell-shocked Pistons team right back into the game with quick shots, nonexistent floor balance and bad transition defense.

The latter part of that contest was especially ugly for Boston, as they allowed 39 points in the final quarter. Their lone remaining superstar, Jayson Tatum, had an awful shooting performance and could not steady his teammates. He missed 17 of his 23 shots and did not provide the much-needed dimension his isolation scoring usually gives Boston from the top of the key. After Jaylen Brown was traded to Philadelphia, the Celtics really do not have that many guys who are comfortable creating their own shot. If Tatum isn’t performing at the All-NBA level he reached before his gruesome Achilles injury, it could become a problem all season long.

First road test for the reigning champions

The one big bright spot for Boston was the play of Paul George, who looked like he wanted to turn back the clock to his old Pacer days. His 38 points were the most ever scored by a Celtic in his debut, and he only needed 21 shots to do it. Not many Bostonians were especially excited to subscribe to the Podcast P experience, but this performance eased at least a few of their worries. Joe Mazzulla’s shot-happy system should suit George quite a bit, and maybe he surprises a lot of people with a solid year.

Besides their two big-name wings, Boston will look to Derrick White and Payton Pritchard to provide most of the scoring. White struggled from the floor in Boston’s first-round playoff loss last season, shooting 32.1 percent, while Pritchard remains one of the elite bench energizers in the entire league. The rest of the Celtics’ rotation includes their three centers, Mitch, Luka Garza and Neemias Queta; a bevy of scrappy younger guys like Hugo Gonzalez, Baylor Scheierman and Jordan Walsh; and elite marksman Sam Hauser. Rookie big Chris Cenac, Mike Conley (yes, he’s still around) and Ron Harper Jr. did not see any action versus Detroit.

Not exactly the scariest bunch on paper, right? Make no mistake, Boston has made a habit of getting consistent results from Mazzulla’s system. They run a professional organization, have a system that more often than not works like a well-oiled machine and have a clear plan for beating their opponent. Tatum is one of the best players in the NBA and surely wants to remind Boston fans that he was the right All-Star wing to build around. So expect a big effort out of him, Mitch and the rest of the Celtics.

For New York, defending the arc and finishing possessions on the glass will be essential, especially with Mitch hunting second chances. Boston’s collapse in Detroit also showed why the Knicks should look to push after misses and take advantage before the Celtics can set their defense. Whatever they throw at New York on Friday won’t surprise our veteran-laden Knickerbockers. But walking into Boston for its home opener and handing the Celtics a second consecutive loss will still be a tall order.

Of course, that’s exactly what we hope to remember from this game. So let’s go Knicks!

Who: New York Knicks (0-1) at Boston Celtics (0-1)Date: Friday, October 23, 2026Place: TD Garden, Boston, MAFollow: @ptknicksblog (X) and @postingandtoasting (BlueSky)

Devin Carter will miss the game for the Celtics with mononucleosis. As of this writing, nothing of note for the Knicks.

items.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
items.author: Guardian sport
items.content:
Max Dowman may get a chance, Spurs need to find balance at Stamford Bridge and Axel Disasi must make amends

After seven games, Nottingham Forest’s record is eerily similar to last season: five points, five goals scored. A year ago Forest’s eighth game was a 3-0 home loss to Chelsea that marked the end for Ange Postecoglou, the second of four managers to occupy the dugout last term. There is no suggestion that Oliver Glasner is under similar scrutiny yet, but the Austrian needs to find solutions for the league’s lowest scorers. Morgan Gibbs-White is available after missing the narrow defeat by Arsenal, while Liam Delap may benefit from a return to familiar surroundings – 12 of his 14 career Premier League goals were scored for Ipswich, six of them at Portman Road. “What we need to improve is getting [Delap] into more positions where he can score,” Glasner said before Friday evening’s game. “He’s one of our best finishers.” Gary O’Neil also lacks a standout scorer, but he is squeezing goals out of his side. Eight different Ipswich players have scored in seven games; only Brighton and Brentford can better that total this season.

items.title: Tour de France 2027 route - The complete stage-by-stage guide
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
The 2027 Tour de France ventures into the United Kingdom for the Grand Départ in Scotland on July 2, and two long stages - to Liverpool and through Wales - before the race lands on home soil.

There are two individual time trials, two major summit finishes, six stages for the sprinters and a load of opportunities for attacks through the Alps, Massif Central and Pyrenees before the race concludes in Paris on July 25 after almost 3,500 kilometres of racing.

Tadej Pogačar will be vying for a record sixth Tour title, but will be challenged by Remco Evenepoel over the 71 kilometres of time trials and by Jonas Vingegaard in the high mountains.

A relatively flat start to the Tour de France could see the first sprinter in the maillot jaune in years, but it's a long and complicated road that's not entirely flat, with some punchy climbs and wind that could foil the sprinters.

  • Côte de Melrose (2.2km at 6.7%), km. 65

This stage is quite long at 223 kilometres and riddled with small climbs that will hamper the sprinters' ability to enjoy the relatively flat finish in Liverpool.

  • Côte de Jubilee Tower (3.8km at 6.1%), km. 88
  • Côte de Trough of Bowland (1.9km at 5.2%), km. 98.5
  • Côte de Waddington Fell (3.4km at 6.4%), km. 112
  • Côte de Belmont (2km at 4%), km. 152.5
  • Côte de Parbold (1.8km at 5.6%), km. 183

Someone should make a one-day Classic out of this 223-kilometre stage from Welshpool to Cardiff. With seven named climbs and a couple of real stingers like the 11% Hengoed climb in the late stages, this one could get very interesting for the GC contenders if they haven't studied up on the style of racing.

  • Côte d'Epynt (3.7km at 7.9%), km. 85.5
  • Côte de Bannau Brycheiniog (6.6km at 3.5%), km. 121.5
  • Côte de Rhigos (4.6km at 5.8%), km. 145.5
  • Côte de Penrhys (1.3km at 10.1%), km. 160.5
  • Côte de Maerdy (1.5km at 8.7%), km. 169
  • Côte de Hengoed (700 m at 11%), km. 197.5
  • Côte de Caerphilly (2km at 8.1%), km. 210.5

A punchy stage to Plumelec is one for the powerful sprinters like Mads Pedersen or Matthew Brennan. The Côte de Cadoudal (1.7km at 6.2%) is climbed twice at the end.

  • Côte de la Croix de la Libération (4.6km at 5.3%), km. 189
  • Signal d'Uchon (5.7km at 5.7%), km. 206.5

One of just two high-altitude summit finishes, the stage to Grand Colombier on stage 9 will be one of the key moments of the 2027 Tour de France.

  • Col du Berthiand (6.3km at 7.5%), km. 57.5
  • Côte des Neyrolles (3.6km at 7.7%), km. 77
  • Col de Richemond (7.7km at 6%), km. 115
  • Grand Colombier (17.4km at 7.1%), km. 162

A preview of the combined 2027 UCI World Championships, stage 10 features the Côte de Domancy twice out of six climbs, making for a tough stage that could well bring some surprises.

  • Col du Plan du Salève (9.6km at 5.4%), km. 26
  • Montée de Brison (5km at 10.2%), km. 74
  • Côte de Domancy (2.5km at 9.4%), km. 111.5
  • Montée du Bettex (5.5km at 8%), km. 126.5
  • Côte du Plateau d'Assy (5.1km at 7.5%), km. 147.5
  • Côte de Domancy (2.5km at 9.4%), km. 162

The third of a difficult string of stages, the finish at le Saisies is just past the summit of the Montée de Bisanne - a fairly steep 12.5km ascent averaging 8.3%. This one has Pogačar written all over it.

  • Col de la Colombière (15.9 km at 7%), km. 16
  • Col de la Croix Fry (7.2 km at 5.5%), km. 40
  • Col de la Forclaz de Queige (5.1 km at 8.2%), km. 85
  • Col du Pré (12.6 km at 7.8%), km. 113
  • Montée de Bisanne (12.4 km at 8.3%), km. 146

The finish in Mende on the Côte de la Croix Neuve a.k.a. Montée Jalabert has produced memorable finishes, starting with Laurent's victory in 1995. It was the place where Joaquim Rodriguez managed to get the better of Alberto Contador in 2010, and where Steve Cummings gave the African team MTN-Qhubeka their first Tour stage win in 2015. Michael Matthews was the last winner here in 2022, but the approach is far more difficult in 2027.

  • Col du Vent (8.4 km at 5.8%), km. 40.5
  • Col de la Lusette (11.6 km at 7.3%), km. 108.5
  • Côte de l'Estrade (5.7 km at 8.3%), km. 175
  • Côte de la Croix Neuve (3 km at 10.1%), km. 197.5

The second individual time trial of the Tour on stage 16 is 33km long and mostly flat, except for a single categorised climb, the Côte de Pech David - a short but steep ascent - in the second half of the race. It only climbs 100m but it does so over just 800m of tarmac.

  • Côte de Pech David (800 m at 12.4%), km. 24

The queen stage of the 2027 Tour de France, stage 18 from Pau to the Col du Portet takes riders over 2000 metres in altitude twice - the first time over the Col du Tourmalet midway through the 174km stage, and then at the finish, with two other medium mountains for good measure.

  • Col du Soulor (11.8 km at 7.3%), km. 50
  • Col du Tourmalet (19 km at 7.4%), km. 106.5
  • Hourquette d'Ancizan (8.2 km at 5.1%), km. 140.5
  • Saint-lary-soulan Col du Portet (16 km at 8.7%), km. 174

The climbing continues on stage 19 with four major ascents including the last chance for glory on the Col de Marie Blanque with 18.5km to go. It's the last major mountain of the Tour since the penultimate stage has been given to the sprinters.

  • Col de Burdincurutcheta (8.7 km at 9.3%), km. 44.5
  • Col de Bagargui (4.8 km at 6.4%), km. 52.5
  • Col de Soudet (15.1 km at 7.2%), km. 95.5
  • Col de Marie Blanque (7.7 km at 8.6%), km. 141.5

After much debate, the Montmartre climb ended up in the final stage of the Tour de France in Paris, with riders tackling the hill, that made its debut in pro cycling during the Olympic Games in 2024, three times. In 2026, the sprinters very nearly caught Mathieu van der Poel, but he held on just long enough to win the stage over teammate Jasper Philipsen.

  • Côte de la Butte Montmartre (1 km à 6.5 %), 74
  • Côte de la Butte Montmartre (1 km à 6.5 %), 90
  • Côte de la Butte Montmartre (1 km à 6.5 %), 106

items.title: Jonas Rutsch and Patrick Eddy add experience for Classics charge for Modern Adventure Factor Racing in 2027
items.author: jackie.tyson@futurenet.com (Jackie Tyson)
items.content:
Australian road race national champion Patrick Eddy and German WorldTour veteran Jonas Rutsch were confirmed as new additions to Modern Adventure Factor Racing in 2027, each signing a one-year contract.

They will join former USPro under-23 road race national champion Owen Cole, who moves from Team Winston Salem-Flow for the next two seasons.

The team debuted at the ProTour level this past season with 20 of the 21 riders signed to two-year deals. Leo Hayter, who was the only team member confirmed for 2026, recently renewed to continue in the burgundy and gold colours through 2027.

Eddy competed as a U23 rider at the Picnic-PostNL programme, earning a promotion from the development squad to the WorldTour team from 2024 to 2025. He competed at the Continental level in 2026 for a breakout year, starting with the Australian title, and then, with Team Brennan, won the overall at Ronde de l'Oise and the Dutch one-day races Midden-Brabant Poort Omloop and Ronde van Overijssel.

"We're thrilled to welcome Jonas to Modern Adventure. He's built for races like Paris-Roubaix and the classics and he brings a whole new level of experience to our team," team Co-founder George Hincapie said in a team press release.

"Pat had a brilliant season, and winning the Australian national title says a lot about the level he’s capable of. He’s also shown he can deliver results in Europe, which is an important quality for our program."

Both Rutsch and Eddy have extensive experience with European racing, that depth important for the team to bolster their Classics campaign.

The US-based squad remains focused on developing North American talent as well and the addition of Cole brings the number of US and Canadian riders to 14.

The 22-year-old from Chapel Hill, North Carolina, joins the team after continuing to establish himself as a versatile young talent. After winning the U23 road national title in 2023, he moved to UAE Team Emirates Gen Z for European racing, earning a podium on the time trial stage at Tour of Sharjah. He returned to a US-based squad for the last two seasons, winning three silver medals at US nationals, as well as a second place on the Mont Mégantic queen stage at Tour de Beauce and GC title at Tour de la Guadeloupe.

“Joining this team as an American feels extra special. Not only is it an organization I think can take me to the next level, it is a project I look forward to being able to say I was a part of,” Owen said in a team statement.

This brings the Modern Adventure Factor roster to 24 riders for 2027, with a final announcement expected next week.

items.title: Tadej Pogačar tops all UCI rankings but one, while Demi Vollering equally dominant in 2026
items.author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
items.content:
For the sixth year in a row, Tadej Pogačar has ended the season as the number one rider in the UCI World Rankings, and his UAE Team Emirates-XRG squad were at the top of the Team Rankings for the fourth straight year.

On the women's side, FDJ United-SUEZ topped the UCI Team Rankings for women for the second year in a row, with World Champion and Tour de France winner Demi Vollering crushing the competition in the individual rankings.

Pogačar and Vollering were nearly tied on points accumulated through the season, with 9,331.75 and 9,330 points, respectively, after both had equally dominant seasons with victories in the Tour de France, Liège-Bastogne-Liège and the Tour of Flanders.

While Vollering had a nearly flawless season, with wins in the Giro d'Italia, Omloop Het Nieuwsblad, La Flèche Wallonne and the World and European Championships road races, Pogačar's season was cut short due to a crash in the Vuelta a España, which meant he gained no points in the World and European Championships.

Still, Pogačar amassed far more points than second-placed Remco Evenepoel (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), who ended the year with the World and European time trial titles, second place in the Tour de France and 7,191.61 points. Next in line were Isaac del Toro (UAE Team Emirates XRG) and Paul Seixas (Decathlon CMA CGM) with 5,606 and 5,580 points, respectively.

Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe were the second-best team, but were over 5,000 points shy of Pogačar's squad, with Visma-Lease a Bike, Decathlon CMA CGM and Lidl-Trek rounding out the top five on the men's side.

Behind Vollering in the women's rankings was Kasia Niewiadoma-Phinney (Canyon-SRAM) with 5,660 points, mirroring her results in the Tour de France and World Championships. Paula Blasi and Elisa Longo Borghini (UAE Team l'IMAD) were third and fourth, and helped their team finish second overall to FDJ by 263 points. SD Worx-Protime, Canyon-SRAM and Visma-Lease a Bike completed the top five. Lorena Wiebes (SD Worx-Protime) was fifth.

In the minor rankings, Pogačar continued his dominance in the UCI Stage Race Rankings, beating Giro d'Italia winner Jonas Vingegaard (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Del Toro, but his three-year winning streak in the UCI One-Day Race Rankings ended because of his crash, and Evenepoel took home that prize for 2026 with Pogačar second and Seixas third.

Pogačar continued to lead the European Tour rankings over Evenepoel and Seixas, but Pinarello-Q36.5 came in as the top team ahead of Tudor and Cofidis. Belgium led the nations rankings.

Biniam Girmay (NSN) led the Africa Tour Rankings ahead of fellow Eritreans Natnael Tesfasion (Movistar) and Henok Mulueberhan (XDS Astana). The Algerian team Madar Pro Cycling led the African team rankings, while Eritrea topped the nations.

In the Americas Tour, Del Toro led the individual rankings ahead of Richard Carapaz (EF Education-EasyPost), with World Champion Brandon McNulty (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) third and, thanks to his rainbow jersey-winning effort, the USA led the nations rankings. Modern Adventure led the team rankings.

Yevgeniy Fedorov (XDS Astana) finished out the year atop the Asia Tour rankings as did his native Kazakhstan, while the Chinese team Li Ning Star led the teams. In Oceania, it was Laurence Pithe, Jai Hindley and Michael Matthews atop the individual rankings, Australia as top nation and CCache X Bodywrap the number one team.

There are no Continental tours for women.

items.title: 'Some haggis and a deep-fried Mars Bar' - Local star Oscar Onley highlights Scottish specialities ahead of 2027 Tour de France
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
Tour de France contender Oscar Onley says he is counting the days to the race's start in Scotland, where the GC specialist will be looking forward to what he calls a "once-in-a-lifetime opportunity" to race cycling's biggest professional event on home soil.

In the meantime, too, he's got every intention highlighting some specialities in the local diet to Tour de France followers who may be unfamiliar with Scottish culinary traditions.

Asked at the Tour de France presentation in Paris on Thursday what people can expect as a Scottish welcome, Onley said - half-jokingly - "Some haggis and a deep-fried Mars Bar, that'd be the go-to.

"It'll be really special, I think, particularly because of the crowds, they always get behind the big sporting events and I expect the same thing next year as well.

"It's something I couldn't even have dreamed of, normally the Tour de France is in France, so it's a once-in-a lifetime opportunity. I really want to hopefully be there, and that's my first goal."

Fourth in the 2025 Tour de France was a breakthrough result for Onley, but then injuries incurred in a major crash on a descent on stage 7 of the Critérium du Dauphiné put paid to his chances of racing it this summer.

Onley subsequently bounced back to take fourth overall in the Vuelta a España, but he denied that there was any extra pressure on him to perform as Ineos have such a significant series of past success in the Tour de France.

"I don't think so. As riders we all put a lot of pressure on ourselves, it's more the team do a good job in managing that and making sure we do everything we need to. But they don't add pressure to what we do."

That said, the goal of winning a Grand Tour remains the main objective for Netcompany Ineos, he argued and "the Tour de France is the biggest one, every team has these big ambitions and we're no different.

"I think from what I've seen in the team this year, we're definitely going in the right direction, we have all the resources to make something like this happen."

Nor are the past Grand Tour victories a distant memory of glories past, he argues, for Netcompany Ineos, with riders who remain in the current lineup also part of the former success in those races.

"Kwiato [Michal Kwiatkowski] is still in the team, he's also been part of a lot of these Tour-winning teams. He's always got lots of stories of training camps and races as well, and it's quite inspiring when he says these things over dinner to us."

The route for 2027 is now out, in any case, and Onley is convinced that having that knowledge so soon, nearly seven months before the event actually starts in Edinburgh next July 2, can only be a good thing. He hasn't yet pinpointed one stage as one that suits him particularly well - although he's certain that'll happen. Rather the idea is to stay in the action in the race from start to finish.

"There are opportunities everywhere, everyone's got weaknesses and strengths and it's better to know the course now, you can really prepare for what's ahead," he reasoned.

"It's not like no-one knows the parcours. There are no excuses for July."

'Where is the Tour de France Hommes?' - Marlen Reusser calls for greater equality between men’s and women’s Tour de France
items.author: Alasdair Fotheringham
items.content:
2026 Tour de France Femmes leader and stage winner Marlen Reusser has made a call to step up the fight for parity between men's and women's cycling, arguing that a great deal has been done but that there are still steps to be taken.

The Movistar leader said she had enjoyed the race presentation in Paris, but argued that there was a greater level of protagonism for the men's event during it than the women's. She also asked why the men's event was not called the Tour de France Hommes to balance it out with the Tour de France Femmes.

ASO organiser Marion Rousse responded to her comments by saying that the race had taken major steps towards a much greater level of equality - something which Reusser had already underlined - but that both the races had to evolve at the same rate as the sport in general. She also pointed out that the Tour de France Femmes presentation was shorter, that was connected to the different length of the events.

Reusser said that she had felt inspired by the route presentation, recalling the time when she had been to a similar kind of event for the Olympics and it had considerably boosted her interest in the event.

"The presentation was really cool, I remember doing after only I was a very short time in cycling, doing the Olympic Games and it was never something I was dreaming about or something, but then I had to go to the kick-off, it was kind of this event in Switzerland for the Olympic Games and I was so infected by the Olympic spirit," she explained.

"So I wanted to come here to see if I get infected and I think that they managed well. It's a nice event."

At the same time, she said, it would be good if things continued to develop in term of the fight for equality between the two events, starting off with their name.

"But I'm a bit disappointed still that it's Tour de France and Tour de France Femmes, where is the Tour de France Hommes? This is weird to me, this I don't understand. Also like we have two nice directors, but I don't feel like it's them on the same level, it's more the men's director that is [on stage] then also having next to him the women's, " she said.

"So I think the Tour is doing so great showing that there is not only men's sport, but then we speak a lot about it but we just should do it more. I wish these little steps to come when we speak about the presentation and the whole thing."

Asked about Reusser's comments, Tour de France Femmes director Marion Rousse argued categorically that there had been a great deal of progress, but warned against taking decisions too fast that could potentially do more harm than good in the long run. She also pointed to the Tour de France Grand Départ in the UK as being a key balancing act between the two races.

"It's already a big first to start in the same country outside the Tour de France, and the United Kingdom is a natural step, because they have already done a lot of work developing with women's sport, with things like the Rugby World Cup in 2025 or the Women's Tour of Britain," Rousse argued. "We're doing exactly the same thing in the UK, three days for the men, three days for the women - it's magnificent.

"We also will continue the work, but there's also the question of continuing to develop the race at the same pace as women's sport. If we suddenly do 15 days of racing tomorrow" - as opposed to the nine in the race as is the case for 2027 - "of course the women are able to do that, but certain teams would find that hard.

"We want to show what women's cycling is capable of doing and that's done, the sponsors are investing and the tv exposure is happening, that's all done. We are going to go on evolving, but we have to be careful, because once a step is taken you can't go back. Each decision is important."

Regarding any perceived imbalance between the men's and the women's presentation, she argued that that was "not really the case, because obviously the men's presentation is going to be longer because there are 21 stages against nine.

"But if not the work is exactly the same and besides we are doing the same thing, it's just there are fewer stages."

items.title: No time trial, Alps, or Pyrenees and a finale that might be without fans – I was left wanting more from the Tour de France Femmes route reveal
items.author: Matilda Price
items.content:
In 2026, the Tour de France Femmes seemed to get everything right. After four years of experimentation, the route felt like ASO had pulled together everything they'd learnt into a beautifully balanced course, featuring a bit of everything: a foreign Grand Départ, an iconic mountain stage, a time trial, and a big-city finale.

The result was a truly thrilling race, delivering six different stage winners, five different riders in the yellow jersey, and a GC battle that went down to the wire on the very last day.

There were limitations, of course, for example the geographical footprint of the race was small, with much of France not getting a chance to by the roadside. But with what ASO and race director Marion Rousse can do with nine days of racing, they seemed to get it pretty spot on.

Fast forward to this year, then, and the expectation around the route reveal was high. How could they build upon perhaps the best edition of the Tour de France Femmes yet? How would they raise the bar again this time, as they have in every other edition? We were surely in for another cracking route.

But when Marion Rousse was done presenting the nine stages that will make up next year's Tour to the Palais de Congrès audience and fans around the world, I was left feeling a bit flat.

My initial reaction to the stage featuring the iconic Puy de Dôme climb was excitement – 'Wow, they're really doing it' – but as the screen faded to black to confirm that was the final stage, my feeling shifted more to 'Oh, is that it?'.

Though not an icon of the 21st century – it was only reintroduced in full to the Tour in 2023 after a 35-year absence – the Puy de Dôme occupies an important place in Tour history, the site of some truly memorable battles, not least when Jacques Anquetil and Raymond Poulidor went literally shoulder to shoulder on the ascent in 1964. Its iconic shape, rising up above Clermont-Ferrand, and the railway following the riders up its slopes gives it a clear and looming identity.

But it's also only 11.3km, only climbs up to 1,415m, and isn't on the level of fame nor difficulty of some of the iconic Pyrenean or Alpine passes. In fact, no climb on the whole 2027 Tour de France Femmes route surpasses 1,500m elevation, let alone the benchmark 2,000m, something you can only get in the Alps and Pyrenees.

It's not that the final three stages aren't packed full of climbing – they are – but there's only so much you can do in France's third biggest mountain range.

Of course, there is a reason to skip the Pyrenees and Alps: the organisers like to change things up each year, and they are also slightly hamstrung by the UK Grand Départ, making the Massif Central much more reasonable to journey to in only a week, compared to going all the way south to either bigger mountain range.

But having seen the true mountain battles we've been treated to for the last few years, the Massif Central – literally and figuratively – just doesn't reach those heights.

In this day and age, 1,400m cannot be the ceiling of how high the Tour de France Femmes can climb. We've known since this race was launched that big, iconic mountains are what make it special, and what deliver the truly showpiece days, like Mont Ventoux earlier this summer.

I have no doubt that this Massif Central-focused course will be challenging, engaging and thrilling, and we'll see another brilliant battle for the yellow jersey – I just wish we were doing it on some bigger, better climbs, more akin to what we've seen before.

It's also an undeniable shame that this race is missing an individual time trial, opting for a team time trial in London as part of the Grand Départ instead. As I wrote in my route explainer, the Tour is limited in time and they can't do everything – at least not in the sense that the men's race can, with a whole 21 stages to play with – so something always has to be dropped.

But is a team time trial really preferable to an individual time trial? It's novel, sure, having never been done in the Tour de France Femmes before, and it's perhaps slightly more fun for casual fans for watch. It also shortens the amount of time that the race will have to close roads in central London for. But is it good for the race?

The results of a TTT will naturally be very different from an ITT, arguably levelling out the playing field between the top riders – they are all both supported and limited by their teammates, so we're unlikely to see a Reusser for example take a bit chunk of time here – but at the same time disproportionately disadvantaging those on smaller teams.

We haven't often seen underdogs come to the fore in the Tour, and including a TTT – which the better-resourced teams always do better in – basically ensures we definitely won't in 2027.

But really, the main issue is that I just think the Tour should have a TT, always. The concept of a men's Tour de France without a time trial is basically unconscionable, and whilst the women's race in only nine stages, it purports to be a Grand Tour, and that should mean the winner has to face a bit of everything: time trialing, sprints, hills and mountains – that's what makes a Grand Tour and a Grand Tour winner.

Riders and teams have long been in agreement on that fact, and have complained when other women's Grand Tours have missed a TT, so for the Tour to go back to a TT-less form feels like a downgrade on last year. A team time trial just isn't the same.

The other really concerning element of the Femmes route reveal is the question over whether fans will be allowed on the Puy de Dôme summit finish.

When the men's race last visited, in 2023, fans were not allowed on the final 4km due to ecological protections, and also the difficulty in getting up the climb that only has one road up, which is flanked on one side by an in-use railway line. That meant the finale of the climb was raced in an eerie absence of spectators, with even very few media at the top to capture the moment, something that perhaps doesn't feel befitting of the biggest race on earth.

But even the risk of having no fans on the final, decisive climb of the race feels fundamentally antithetical to everything the Tour de France Femmes has been building for the last five years. The whole project has been based around , bringing fans out, making the event as big and as accessible as possible to show just how much appetite there is for women's racing.

Mont Ventoux this year was a spectacular example of that, with fans lining every kilometre of the Bald Mountain, making the long journey up to its moon-like peak. The fans are what have made this race so special and successful, and has always been at the heart of the event.

So to not have fans present to cheer on the sport's best athletes on the decisive, climactic climb of next year's race would not just be disappointing, it would be a failure in organisation. We'll all be keeping our fingers crossed that ASO and the local authorities find a solution, but if they don't, and we have a fan-free finale to the biggest race on earth next summer, serious questions will have to be asked over the decisionmaking around going to this particular climb.

I thought that ASO finally cracked the formula on how to do it all within nine days in 2026, but 2027's route has shown us that truly doing a little bit of everything, including a TT, and going to one of the big two mountain ranges, is still a stretch for this race. Which is understandable, but when we've seen how good it can be, it's hard to not feel a little shortchanged.

I know the race will deliver, it always does, but on paper, it's left a lot to be desired.

items.title: 'I will pour my heart and soul into becoming a better rider’ - Mountain bike star Jolanda Neff makes surprise move to Fenix-Premier Tech
items.author: Owen Rogers
items.content:
Former mountain bike world and Olympic champion Jolanda Neff will ride on the Fenix-Premier Tech squad for two years from 2027, the Belgian team have announced.

At 33-years-old, the Swiss rider is experienced across road and cyclo-cross, but she is best known for her exploits on the mountain bike, a discipline where she has gained a wealth of success.

Not only did she win Olympic gold in Tokyo, she was cross-country World Champion in 2017 and the cross-country MTB Marathon rainbow jersey winner the year before that. She also boasts 16 elite World Cup race victories in her career.

While Neff might not have been quite as successful on the cyclo-cross field, she has a total of 11 wins, with two last season when she was competitive in every race she rode.

On the road, Neff has never won above .2 level, but as long ago as 2014 she bagged third place at Trofeo Alfredo Binda, then a top-level World Cup race, and was fourth and fifth on general classification at the UCI Women’s WorldTour stage race, Tour de Suisse, in 2021 and 2022, respectively.

Neff has raced the last two mountain bike campaigns for the Cannondale Factory Racing outfit, but that team’s demise, which coincides with the company’s move to the Netherlands, has forced her to seek a team elsewhere, and Fenix-Premier Tech seems a good fit.

"I’m really excited to join Fenix-Premier Tech, a team that unites mountain biking, cyclocross and road racing at a world-class level," Neff said in a team statement.

"I will pour my heart and soul into becoming a better rider in every aspect, as well as sharing all my experience with other riders. I have always admired how this team puts a strong focus on women and on creating professional structures for them, as well as developing young riders with a long-term vision. I hope to make a great contribution to Fenix-Premier Tech and can’t wait to get racing!"

Fenix-Premier Tech and their brother team Alpecin-Premier Tech, are a true multi-discipline outfit with a number of riders throughout the roster riding both on and off-road. On the women’s side alone, the team boasts cyclo-cross World Cup race winners Aniek van Alphen and Puck Pieterse, as well as former World Champion Ceylin de Carmen Alvarado. Pieterse is also a past mountain bike World Champion, and has won the best young rider and mountains classifications at the Tour de France Femmes avec Zwift, along with a handful of top Classics.

items.title: Visma say 'there could have been more' summit finishes on 2027 Tour de France route, but remain certain of opportunities for two-time winner Jonas Vingegaard
items.author: James Moultrie
items.content:
Visma-Lease a Bike see plenty of opportunities for their leaders at the 2027 Tour de France, where they will likely be led by two-time winner Jonas Vingegaard, who crashed out of this year's edition, Wout van Aert, and potentially sprinter Matthew Brennan.

After the route was revealed on Thursday in Paris, Head of Racing Marc Reef commented on the 21 stages, where two time trials, six mountain stages, and a brutal queen stage in the Pyrenees are set to decide the next yellow jersey.

“At first glance, it looks like a fairly balanced route, with several flat sprint stages, explosive finales and tough mountain stages," said Reef.

"The two long, relatively flat time trials stand out in particular. It’s been a long time since we’ve had that in the Tour. Compared to last year, I count fewer summit finishes, and in my opinion, there could have been more. All in all, it’s an interesting route."

To Reef's point, there are only three summit finishes on the 2027 course: stage 9 to Grand Colombier, stage 11 to Les Saisies, and stage 18 to Saint-Lary-Soulan Col du Portet.

On paper, it's a route more in favour of this year's runner-up Remco Evenepoel than Vingegaard, but it's defending champion Tadej Pogačar that both riders will be looking to knock off top spot in July.

Reef noted how important the two time trials will be for GC, totalling 71 kilometres, but also how the days to Sallanches and up the Col du Portet will be crucial as Vingegaard looks to defeat Pogačar for the first time since 2023.

"[Stages 9 to 11 are] where the GC contenders will go head-to-head for the first time. These are stages that could suit us well. Racing on the World Championships course also adds an extra dimension to the Tour," he said.

“The last time we had this many [ITT kilometres] was in 2012. On top of that, most of the courses are relatively flat. Time trialling is a discipline we work on extensively and invest a lot in. We’re generally very strong in this area, and we have several specialists on the team. These races against the clock will play a major role in the general classification.

The Pyrenees duo of stages are "where the race will be decided”, according to Reef, on stages 18 and 19. With 5,400m of elevation gain on the former, it's not only the hardest stage of the 114th edition, but one of the most difficult in recent memory, and would be somewhere where a top-form Vingegaard should thrive.

"Some television viewers may find it harder to relate to the climbs on this year’s Tour de France route, but there are still some fantastic stages. The finishes atop the Grand Colombier and Col de Portet are certainly ones to look forward to. The final stage in Paris is another highlight, of course," said Reef.

"It looks like a route that should suit several of our riders very well. Our task now is to analyse the route thoroughly and use that analysis to develop a plan that gives us the best possible chance of success as a team. One thing is certain: this route offers us plenty of opportunities to achieve great things."

The Tour kicks off on July 2 in 2027, with a flat stage from Edinburgh in Scotland to Carlisle in England, where they could bring Brennan as a debutant, alongside his superstar lead-out man from the Vuelta, Van Aert – who will no doubt get his own opportunities on the plethora of punchy stages – and target the first yellow jersey with the Brit on home roads.
